title: GTM Revenue Engine Score
subtitle: Measures how far your B2B marketing has evolved from tracking activity to running a full revenue engine: AI-assisted, account-precise, and built to scale without adding headcount.

questions.text: When you present marketing performance to the CEO or board, what is the primary metric on slide one?

answers.label: Impressions, reach, or follower growth
MQL volume and email open rates
SQLs and total pipeline created
Pipeline influenced and revenue contribution broken down by channel
Marketing-sourced revenue, CAC, and payback period tied to one attribution model

questions.text: How are marketing targets set at your company?

answers.label: Activity targets: posts published, emails sent, events organized
Lead volume targets (MQLs) owned by marketing alone
SQL and pipeline targets handed down from sales leadership
Shared pipeline target negotiated and agreed between marketing and sales
Co-owned revenue quota — marketing and sales measured on the same number

questions.text: When you lose a deal, how much do you know about which marketing touchpoints were part of the journey?

answers.label: Almost nothing — we hear about the loss through sales after the fact
We can see if a contact was ever in a campaign, but the path is unclear
We track first-touch and last-touch but not the full buying committee journey
We have multi-touch attribution and know which channels influenced the deal
We can reconstruct the full buying committee journey: every touchpoint, every stakeholder

low.headline: Marketing is an island. Fix the revenue wiring first.
low.text: Right now marketing generates activity and sales generates revenue. Those are two separate stories. CEOs nod at lead numbers, then ask about revenue — and that gap is where marketing credibility goes to die. Before you change any campaign or tool, fix how success is defined and measured.
steps: Book a 30-minute session with your CRO or head of sales to agree on a shared pipeline definition. One number you are both measured on.
Implement basic multi-touch attribution in your CRM before your next board review.
Replace your top-line MQL report with a pipeline-created and revenue-influenced table. A spreadsheet is fine to start.

mid.headline: You are speaking revenue. Now make it automatic.
mid.text: You have the right metrics on the table and the right conversations happening. The next bottleneck is speed: you are probably still pulling these numbers by hand or waiting on sales ops to run reports. AI-native teams fix this in the data layer, not the reporting layer.
steps: Automate your pipeline and attribution reports so they are live, not compiled weekly.
Define a marketing-sourced versus marketing-influenced split your CFO will sign off on. Remove the ambiguity.
Set up a shared Slack channel with sales leadership that surfaces deal signals in real time.

high.headline: You are running at board level. Now optimize the engine.
high.text: Revenue attribution is solved. The opportunity now is velocity: using that data to kill losing plays faster and double down on what is working, without waiting for a quarterly review.
steps: Build a campaign performance dashboard that flags underperformers within 72 hours, not 3 weeks.
Run a CAC cohort analysis by channel and cut the bottom quartile before next quarter.
Present a marketing-to-revenue waterfall at your next leadership meeting: channel by channel, with payback period.

questions.text: How integrated is your current GTM tech stack?

answers.label: Tools work in isolation — data lives in separate platforms with no sync
CRM and email are connected but reporting is still manually compiled
Most tools share data but we still rely on spreadsheets for key decisions
Stack is integrated and most reporting is automated with minimal manual work
Single revenue data layer: one source of truth, real-time, AI-assisted interpretation

questions.text: How does AI currently operate in your GTM workflows?

answers.label: Occasional ad-hoc use by individuals: ChatGPT for copy, nothing systematic
A few team members use AI tools personally, not embedded in any team workflow
AI is embedded in 2 to 3 specific processes: content, prospecting, or reporting
AI runs multiple GTM workflows and we track its measurable impact on output and speed
AI is wired into the full revenue engine: content, targeting, scoring, and reporting all have live AI layers

questions.text: How many hours per week does your marketing team collectively spend on manual reporting, data pulls, and dashboard updates?
questions.hint: Count all team hours: pulling platform data, building slides, updating trackers. We use €80/hr as the loaded cost reference for a mid-senior marketing hire in Central/Western Europe — this is used in the cost calculation below.

low.headline: Your stack is costing more than it saves. Start with the data layer.
low.text: Disconnected tools and manual reporting are not just inefficient — they delay decisions. By the time you have compiled the report, the window to act has already closed. AI-native GTM teams run at a fraction of the tool count, with everything wired together into one revenue layer.
steps: Audit your current stack: list every tool, its monthly cost, and how often the team actually uses it. Cut anything that is not wired to revenue data.
Pick one reporting workflow to automate this month. The goal is zero manual compilation, not a perfect dashboard.
Run a small AI pilot in one workflow (content drafts, lead scoring, or follow-up sequencing) and measure before-versus-after output time.

mid.headline: Good foundation. Now systematize the AI layer.
mid.text: You have built the connections. The next move is shifting AI from a productivity tool to a revenue tool: embedded in how you score accounts, surface intent signals, and decide where to spend the next campaign budget.
steps: Map every manual decision your team makes weekly and identify which ones could run on a model or a rule.
Connect your AI tooling to your CRM so insights are pushed to where sales actually works, not sitting in a separate dashboard.
Define one AI use case that directly touches pipeline (lead scoring, buying signal detection, account prioritization) and run it for 60 days.

high.headline: You are running an AI-assisted engine. Now build the moat.
high.text: A single person with the right AI stack can now ship what took a full team 6 months ago. You are close. The move that creates real distance is proprietary data: your own signals, your own scoring logic that competitors cannot replicate by buying the same SaaS tools.
steps: Start capturing proprietary behavioral signals (content engagement patterns, deal velocity by persona, repeat touchpoints) that feed your own models.
Document your AI workflow stack and run a quarterly audit. What was new 6 months ago is likely already a standard feature in the market.
Build one automation that removes a full headcount-equivalent task from the team's plate this quarter.

questions.text: How does your company appear in AI-driven search results (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google AI Overviews)?

answers.label: We have never checked — we do not know if we appear at all
We show up occasionally but cannot explain why or how to influence it
We have audited our GEO/AEO presence, found the gaps, but have no strategy yet
We have a content strategy specifically designed to appear in AI search on our key topics
We are consistently surfaced in AI responses for our target topics and we track it as a channel

questions.text: How strong and consistent is your company's point of view in the market?

answers.label: We publish content, mostly product updates and curated industry news
We write thought leadership occasionally but the angle and voice shift between authors
We have a defined POV documented internally, but it is not consistently visible in our public content
We publish a consistent POV and peers in our space actively reference us for it
Our POV sets the conversation in our niche: buyers and analysts cite us, not just follow us

questions.text: Who carries your company's commercial voice in the market?

answers.label: The marketing team posts on brand channels — leadership rarely appears publicly
Marketing plus occasional LinkedIn posts from the CEO, with no coordinated strategy
Two or three executives post regularly but each runs their own content without a GTM link
We run an active founder-led or executive-led content program with clear pipeline intent
Founder-led selling and B2B influencer content are tracked, optimized, and our top pipeline source

low.headline: When content production cost hits zero, who said it matters more than what was said.
low.text: GenAI flooded every B2B channel with empty content. If your company's voice is not distinctive and consistently out in the market, you are invisible — not just to buyers but to the AI search engines now shaping how they discover you. This is a distribution problem, not a content quality problem.
steps: Write down your company's three non-obvious beliefs about your market: the takes most competitors will not say out loud. That is your starting POV.
Run an AI search audit: ask ChatGPT and Perplexity what they say about your category, your competitors, and your company. Map the gap.
Get the founder or CEO to commit to two posts per week for 90 days: not marketing-approved brand content, but real opinions backed by what you have built and seen.

mid.headline: You have a voice. Now build the distribution engine around it.
mid.text: You have content and a point of view. What is missing is the system: a way to convert that content into consistent GEO presence, inbound signals, and named leads that show up in your pipeline. Good content without a capture layer is reach without revenue.
steps: Audit your top 10 content pieces: which ones are structured to appear in AI search results (clear questions, direct answers, structured data)? Rebuild the bottom half.
Add a capture mechanism to every high-performing content piece: a comment trigger, a DM link, or a form that ties back to pipeline.
Build a 30-day editorial calendar that connects your POV to active buying signals in your pipeline. Write toward the deals, not the industry trends.

high.headline: You are building a content moat. Protect and systematize it.
high.text: You are doing what most B2B marketing teams cannot: turning authority into pipeline. The risk at this stage is key-person dependency. If your POV lives in one person's head, you are one departure away from losing the asset.
steps: Document your content POV framework so it can scale across multiple voices on your team without diluting the angle.
Track GEO/AEO performance monthly: which queries are you winning, which did you lose this quarter, and what is the content gap to close?
Build a B2B influencer or partner co-content program. Your audience is their audience, and co-posts consistently outperform single-author on reach and trust signals.

questions.text: How precisely are your demand gen campaigns targeted?

answers.label: Broad targeting: any company that loosely fits a description of our market
We have an ICP definition but campaigns still run to large, loosely filtered lists
We have a defined ICP and tiered target account list, mostly inbound execution
Named account programs with personalized outreach coordinated between marketing and sales
Full ABM motion: tiered account list, buying committee mapped per account, plays triggered by real-time intent data

questions.text: How do you address the full buying committee in a typical B2B deal?

answers.label: We target the main decision-maker and assume they will manage internal buy-in
We create content for different roles occasionally but have no coordinated multi-stakeholder approach
We have mapped the typical buying committee (6 to 11 people) and have content for each role
We run coordinated programs touching each committee member by role with relevant content
We track committee-level engagement per account and trigger sales plays based on multi-stakeholder signals

questions.text: How does your outbound motion perform compared to three years ago?

answers.label: Worse: reply rates have dropped sharply and we are not sure why
Flat: we are sending more volume to maintain the same results
We have moved toward more personalized outreach and seen some improvement
We rebuilt our outbound around intent signals and buying triggers: results are back up
Outbound is a minor part of our pipeline. Inbound and referral now dominate.

low.headline: Templated outbound gets zero response. You need account-level targeting.
low.text: The marketing playbooks that worked 3 years ago are dead. GenAI flooded every B2B channel. Broad targeting and spray-and-pray outbound do not just underperform — they damage your domain reputation and burn your best contacts. Precision beats volume every time now.
steps: Run a win/loss analysis on your last 20 closed deals. Map the ICP characteristics of the 10 you won. That is your real target, not your stated one.
Build a named account list of 50 to 100 companies before your next campaign. If you cannot name them, you do not have a target — you have a description.
Stop sending the same message to 5,000 contacts. Pick 20 accounts this month and run a fully personalized 3-touch sequence per buying committee role.

mid.headline: Good targeting. Now wire in the buying committee layer.
mid.text: You are running account-based. But if you are still selling to one contact per account, you are leaving deals on the table. B2B buying committees average 6 to 11 people. Decisions happen in places you cannot track. The teams winning deals now show up for every stakeholder, not just the champion.
steps: Map the buying committee structure for your top 20 target accounts: identify the champion, the budget holder, the technical evaluator, and the likely blocker.
Build one content piece per committee role that addresses the specific objection each role brings to the table.
Set up account-level intent scoring in your CRM that aggregates signals from all contacts at an account, not just your main contact.

high.headline: You are running ABM properly. Now automate the signal layer.
high.text: Named accounts, mapped committees, coordinated plays. That is the playbook. The next level is intent data operating in real time: knowing when an account is active before they fill out a form, and getting the right play in front of sales before the window closes.
steps: Integrate a third-party intent data source (G2, Bombora, LinkedIn Insights) with your CRM and define threshold triggers for sales escalation.
Build an account health score that weights buying committee engagement, not just individual contact activity.
Run a quarterly ABM review: which account tiers are converting, which are not, and what is the committee penetration rate (contacts reached versus total committee size)?

questions.text: When a new GTM approach gets proposed (new channel, new message, new ICP segment), how does your team evaluate it?

answers.label: We discuss it in planning meetings and decide based on gut feel and past experience
We add it to next quarter's roadmap and test it when capacity allows
We can usually run a small test within 4 to 6 weeks if it clears an internal review
We have a fast-test framework: lightweight experiments are live within 2 weeks
New approaches go live in days. We validate with real data before committing budget.

questions.text: How does your team learn and adapt from underperforming campaigns?

answers.label: We move on to the next thing: there is no formal retrospective process
We discuss what went wrong in team meetings but rarely change the approach as a result
We run post-mortems on major campaigns and update our playbook once a quarter
We have a documented test-learn cycle: hypotheses logged, results captured, playbook updated in real time
AI-assisted analysis surfaces learnings automatically. Our playbook updates after every campaign, not quarterly.

questions.text: How many weeks does it typically take from 'let's test this GTM approach' to having your first real data back?
questions.hint: Count from when the idea is agreed on to the point you have enough data to make a go/no-go call. We calculate the cost using 3 GTM contributors × 40 hrs/week × €80/hr loaded cost versus a 1-week AI-native baseline — this drives the figure shown below. AI-native teams typically land at 1 to 2 weeks.

low.headline: Your validation cycle is a competitive liability.
low.text: AI-native GTM teams validate new approaches in days, not quarters — with a fraction of the resources. If it takes 6 to 8 weeks to know whether a new channel works, you will run 2 experiments a year while a faster competitor runs 20. Speed of learning is the compounding advantage in modern GTM.
steps: Define a minimum viable test standard for your team: what is the smallest version of this idea that gives you real signal within 2 weeks?
Remove the approval layers that slow down small experiments. Anything under a defined budget threshold should not need committee sign-off.
Pick one campaign running right now and build a 72-hour checkpoint into it: what do the early signals say, and would you still make the same call with that data?

mid.headline: Good testing culture. Now build the institutional memory.
mid.text: You are running experiments. The question is whether the team actually learns from them and carries those findings into the next decision. Most teams test, then forget. The ones that win build a compounding knowledge base where last quarter's failure makes next quarter's test faster and cheaper.
steps: Build a shared experiment log: hypothesis, setup, result, decision — 5 lines per test, owned by whoever ran it.
Before launching any new campaign, require a 10-minute review of the three most relevant past experiments and what they showed.
Automate the learning extraction: set up an AI-assisted synthesis that pulls campaign data and surfaces the key signal without a manual report.

high.headline: You are running at market speed. Now build the flywheel.
high.text: Fast validation is a real edge in B2B GTM right now. The teams moving at this pace are the ones reshaping how buyers discover, evaluate, and buy in their categories. The next step is not faster — it is building the proprietary playbook that competitors cannot copy because it is built from your data, not a shared methodology.
steps: Document your test-learn framework formally. It should be the first thing a new GTM hire reads on day one.
Build a forecast model that factors in experiment velocity, not just pipeline coverage. Show leadership what 2x more tests per quarter is worth in revenue terms.
Share one validated insight from your GTM experiments publicly every quarter. It is an authority signal and a recruiting signal at the same time.

cta.headline: Want a partner who turns this score into an actual plan?
cta.description: Most people don't fail at the assessment. They fail at sequencing. In 30 minutes I'll show you which two things to fix first, based on your score and your stage. No pitch deck, just the sequencing call.
